To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
GK is regulated by tissue-specific transcriptional and posttranslational control mechanisms, which determine its glucose sensor function in liver and pancreatic beta cells.
GK is a bifunctional enzyme with a low affinity for its substrate glucose.

the glucose sensor function of the low-affinity glucose-6-phosphorylase glucokinase (hexokinase IV) in liver and pancreatic beta-cells results from a complex regulatory network that includes transcriptionally and posttranslational regulated levels of the enzyme and its regulatory protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of glucose sensor function and glucose homeostasis in liver and pancreatic islets.
the elucidation of the complex regulatory network of GK in liver, pancreatic β-cells, and neuroendocrine cells.
the identification and characterization of regulatory mechanisms of GK in liver, pancreatic β-cells, and other tissues.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GK regulatory network in β-cells is not yet fully understood and that more research in this area is warranted.
GK is not a simple enzyme, but a complex and multifunctional protein.

the regulatory mechanisms in liver and β-cell GK differ significantly, and this is the basis for the different roles that these two isoforms of GK play in glucose homeostasis and in glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GK is a glucose sensor in liver, pancreatic β-cells, and the brain.

the GK regulatory network is an intricate system of transcriptional, posttranslational, and catalytic mechanisms that have to be understood in order to develop novel therapeutic strategies for type 2 diabetic patients.
